claims.text: Constituent count alone does not explain the mechanical-property differences among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Magnetic interactions differ between the ternary and quinary alloys.
Differences in magnetic interactions control the ease of deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Mn experiences magnetic frustration in the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy because its preferred antiparallel spin alignment cannot be completely satisfied.
Magnetic frustration depends on alloy composition and can be modified by changing Mn content.
Mn-induced magnetic frustration stabilizes the FCC phase in the quinary alloy.
Mn-induced magnetic frustration suppresses deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation in the quinary alloy.
Reducing or eliminating Mn lowers magnetic frustration in the proposed ternary or quaternary derivatives.
Lower magnetic frustration reduces the energy barrier for an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Dislocation activity triggers localized nanoscale HCP formation at slip bands.
The Mn-reduced alloys will undergo more deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation than the quinary baseline.
Greater FCC-to-HCP transformation will increase the strain-hardening rate.
Greater FCC-to-HCP transformation will improve the balance of strength and ductility.
Nanoscale HCP regions alter failure behavior.
All compared alloys will be prepared as equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials using identical thermomechanical processing.
The comparison will use identical room-temperature tensile conditions and similar strain rates.
The transformed HCP regions can be monitored during deformation by high-resolution microscopy or in situ diffraction.
Under the proposed controls, only the compositional difference, particularly Mn content, will influence transformation behavior.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that only Mn content differs, but the proposed equiatomic Cr-Co-Ni and Cr-Fe-Co comparisons remove more than one quinary constituent and raise the retained elements from 20 at.% to about 33.3 at.%. Thus Mn content is not independently varied, and the comparison cannot isolate Mn as written.
